title: Karna looks at the sun
hookLine: Karna strings the bow, one sentence stops him, and he looks up at Surya, the father he doesn't know
carry: surya, the sun, sees what the arena can't

cards: As the kings give up, one by one, a man rises whom we've met before. Karna. Found in a basket on the river, raised by a charioteer, born with armor on his body.
The bow has just thrown kings to the floor in front of everyone. Karna walks up to it.

teach.h: I WILL NOT CHOOSE A SUTA.
teach.b: In the version Ganguli translated, Karna lifts the bow and strings it. He fits the arrows. He's about to shoot.
And Draupadi speaks, loudly, so the whole arena hears. In paraphrase: I will not choose a suta for my husband. A suta: a charioteer, a charioteer's son.
Karna laughs, a bitter laugh, the text says. He glances up at the sun, and puts the bow down.

Readers hear Draupadi's line in different ways: holding the contest to the terms her brother read out, which counted birth; guarding her father's hope for Arjuna; or the old sting of birth used against a man who could clearly do the thing.
The poem doesn't settle it. But stay with the glance.
The sun, as we know and the arena doesn't, is Karna's father: Surya, the sun god. And for Hindus the sun isn't only a star.

teach.h: SURYA, THE EYE OF THE GODS.
teach.b: In the Rig Veda, Surya is the eye of the gods, the one who sees everything. Hindus still greet him every morning: pouring water toward the rising sun, an offering called arghya, or bowing to him in Surya namaskar.
Later in this poem, Karna himself is a devoted worshipper of the sun. So here's what this moment holds. The arena looks at Karna and sees a charioteer's son.

teach.h: SURYA SEES WHAT THE ARENA CAN'T.
teach.b: Surya, who sees everything, sees his own son. And Karna looks up to him at the moment he's turned away, without knowing whose face he's looking for.
Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall, later in this serial. For now the bow is back on the ground, and the arena waits for someone else.

how: Many Hindus offer water to the rising sun each morning, called arghya, and in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh the festival of Chhath is given to Surya; Karna's story is retold in storytelling, theater, dance and novels.

s: in this version he strings it and fits the arrows before Draupadi speaks.
Karna was raised by a charioteer
Adhiratha and his wife Radha found him on the river and raised him.
for Hindus the sun is only a star that lights the day
Surya is a god, called in the Rig Veda the eye of the gods; many Hindus greet him with water every dawn.

games.q: a friend asks why Karna looked at the sun when Draupadi turned him away. by what you learned, what fits?
o: the sun is Surya, his unknown father, who sees everything the arena can't.
he was checking the time to see if the contest was over.
he was asking for the strength to shoot anyway.
games.why: the text gives him no words, only a bitter laugh and a glance at the sun. the arena saw a suta's son; Surya, all-seeing, saw his own.

practice: If you can, face a window or the morning light. Many Hindus greet the sun at dawn by pouring a little water toward it, arghya, and saying Om suryaya namah, I bow to the sun.
If you have water, hold a cup and do the same, and if you pray, add one thing you wish someone could see in you. If you don't pray, just feel the light on your face for a few breaths.
It shines on you no matter what anyone calls you.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's swayamvara. Today, Karna at the bow, one sentence from the princess, and a glance at the sun.

orig.note: Sanskrit sūta: a charioteer; the word Draupadi uses for Karna, who was raised by one.

carryVoice: Your line: Surya, the sun, sees what the arena can't. Karna looked up to a father he didn't know. That's day seven hundred forty-two.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Swayamvara Parva (Karna strings the bow; Draupadi refuses a suta; Karna glances at the sun and puts the bow down)
Rig Veda 1.115.1 and 1.50 (Surya, the eye of Mitra, Varuna and Agni; the all-seeing sun)
